prompt: Why does `BookService` throw `DuplicateIsbnException` instead of answering a 409 itself?
hint: Which layer knows what HTTP is?

choices.text: A 409 is the web layer's word, and the rule is the shop's
choices.why: Right. "An ISBN appears once" is true for a controller, an import job or a test alike, so the service states it in the shop's words and the web layer translates.

choices.text: Spring forbids a `@Service` from returning a `ResponseEntity`
choices.why: Nothing forbids it, and it would compile and run. The objection is design: the service would then speak HTTP to callers that are not web requests at all.

choices.text: Throwing is quicker than building a response object
choices.why: Speed is not the reason. Creating an exception captures a stack trace, which costs more than building a small object, not less.

choices.text: Only an exception handler can produce a 409
choices.why: A controller can return `ResponseEntity.status(409)` directly, the way lesson 6's `get` returned its 404. The lesson moves that job out of the controller on purpose.

prompt: The service throws `BookNotFoundException` now, and `ApiErrorHandler` does not exist yet. What does `GET /books/99` answer?
hint: Lesson 6's `Optional` handling is gone, and nothing claims the exception.

choices.text: 404 with an empty body, as in lesson 6
choices.why: That 404 came from the controller turning an empty `Optional` into `ResponseEntity.notFound()`. The controller no longer does that; the exception goes straight through it.

choices.text: 404 with the exception's message as the body
choices.why: Turning the exception into a 404 is exactly what is missing. Nothing in the application maps `BookNotFoundException` to any status yet.

choices.text: 500 from Spring Boot's error page
choices.why: Right. The exception crossed Spring MVC unclaimed, and Boot's error page answered the only way it can for that: the server failed.

choices.text: Nothing: the application refuses to start without a handler
choices.why: Spring does not check at startup that every exception has a handler. An exception happens per request, and this one became a 500.

prompt: Why do `BookNotFoundException` and `DuplicateIsbnException` extend `RuntimeException` rather than `Exception`?
hint: Think about the controller that sits between the service and the client.

choices.text: `@ExceptionHandler` accepts unchecked exceptions and no others
choices.why: An `@ExceptionHandler` can name any exception type, checked or not. The choice is about the code between the throw and the handler.

choices.text: A checked exception cannot carry a message
choices.why: Both kinds pass a message to `super`, exactly as these two classes do.

choices.text: Spring Boot logs unchecked exceptions and ignores checked ones
choices.why: Logging does not depend on that. Boot logged the 500 because nothing handled the exception, and it would have logged a checked one the same way.

choices.text: So the controller need not catch or declare them
choices.why: Right. A checked exception would force every method on the way to handle or declare it. Lesson 14 adds a second reason: Spring rolls a transaction back on a `RuntimeException` by default and not on a checked one.

prompt: Two requests with the same new ISBN reach `BookService.add` at the same instant, with the in-memory repository. What can happen?
hint: `add` is a check and then a save: two steps.

choices.text: The second waits for the first, because the map is a concurrent one
choices.why: `ConcurrentSkipListMap` makes each single operation safe. It does nothing to make the pair "look, then save" one step.

choices.text: Both pass the check, and the ISBN is stored twice
choices.why: Right. Each request checks before either has saved. Lesson 9's table closes the gap with a `UNIQUE` constraint, which the database enforces whatever the timing.

choices.text: Spring hands requests to a service bean one at a time
choices.why: The service is a single shared bean, and Tomcat runs requests on several threads at once, all calling it.

choices.text: The second always gets a 409, since the check is in the service
choices.why: The check is in the service, but it only sees what has been saved. Neither request has saved anything when both check.

prompt: Match each member of an RFC 9457 problem document to what it holds.
hint: One is for programs, one is for this occurrence, one never changes for a kind.

pairs.right: a URI naming the kind of problem, which a program compares
a short summary, the same every time the kind occurs
an explanation of this occurrence, for a person

prompt: A mobile app must show a "this ISBN is already listed" screen when adding a book fails for that reason. Which member of the problem should it test?
hint: Which member is still the same after somebody rewords the sentences?

choices.text: `detail`, because it names the ISBN
choices.why: `detail` is written for a person and may be reworded at any time. An app that matches its words breaks on the day it is, with no error anywhere.

choices.text: `status`, because a 409 means a duplicate
choices.why: 409 means a conflict with the current state, and more than one kind of problem can share it: lesson 14 adds a 409 for a book that is out of stock.

choices.text: `type`
choices.why: Right. It names the kind of problem and is the member the RFC means programs to compare: here `https://bookshop.example/problems/duplicate-isbn`.

choices.text: `title`, because it is short and fixed
choices.why: `title` is the same for every occurrence, but it is still text for people, free to be reworded or translated. `type` is the identifier.

prompt: What status code did the bookshop answer when it was sent a second book with ISBN `9786500000016`?
hint: The request was valid; it conflicted with the catalogue.

prompt: Nothing in `ApiErrorHandler` sets `instance`, yet the 404 for book 99 carried `"instance": "/books/99"`. Where did it come from?
hint: The handler left one member empty.

choices.text: Spring filled in the request's path
choices.why: Right. When a returned `ProblemDetail` has no `instance`, Spring MVC sets it to the path of the request being answered.

choices.text: `forStatusAndDetail` copies the request's URL into it
choices.why: `forStatusAndDetail` sets `status` and `detail` and nothing else. It never sees the request.

choices.text: Jackson adds an `instance` member to every object it writes
choices.why: Jackson writes the members an object has. A `BookResponse` gets no `instance`.

choices.text: Tomcat appends it to the body of every error
choices.why: Tomcat does not touch the body. The member that looks like it, `path`, belongs to Spring Boot's own error page, a different shape altogether.

prompt: An RFC 9457 error body is sent with the media type `application/___+json`.
What does extending `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` give `ApiErrorHandler`?
hint: Whose exceptions does the base class know about?

choices.text: A handler for every exception, the bookshop's own included
choices.why: It knows nothing about `BookNotFoundException`, which needed a method of its own, and an unexpected exception still reached Spring Boot's error page.

choices.text: The `@RestControllerAdvice` annotation, inherited from the base class
choices.why: The annotation is written on `ApiErrorHandler` itself. Without it the class would not be an advice at all, whatever it extended.

choices.text: The validation of request bodies
choices.why: `@Valid` and Bean Validation do the validating, as in lesson 6. The base class only answers the failure.

choices.text: Handlers for Spring MVC's own exceptions, in the problem shape
choices.why: Right: a body that is not JSON, a path nobody maps, a wrong method or media type, a failed validation, all in the same shape as the bookshop's errors.

prompt: Match each request to the status the rebuilt bookshop answered it with.
hint: Each status is the one HTTP has for the case.

pairs.left: `POST /books` with a body that is not JSON

prompt: The 400 for a body that is not JSON has no `type` member. What does the RFC say an absent `type` means?
hint: Spring omits one particular value when it writes the JSON.

choices.text: `about:blank`: nothing beyond what the status code itself says
choices.why: Right. Spring leaves `type` at `about:blank` and omits it, and `title` is then the status's own phrase, "Bad Request".

choices.text: The server forgot it, so the document is invalid
choices.why: All five members are optional, and an absent `type` has a defined meaning rather than being a mistake.

choices.text: The client has to read `detail` to learn the kind
choices.why: There is no further kind to learn: the problem is what the status code says. Reading `detail` is the habit the lesson warns against.

choices.text: The server does not know what happened, as with a 500
choices.why: It knows exactly: the body could not be read. That is a client error with nothing more specific to name.

prompt: Which of these answers from the rebuilt bookshop carried a header saying what the server would have accepted? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them list what would have worked.

choices.text: The 405 for `DELETE /books/1`
choices.why: Right: `Allow: GET` lists the methods `/books/1` takes.

choices.text: The 404 for `GET /nope`
choices.why: A 404 has nothing to list. Its headers were only `Content-Type`, `Transfer-Encoding` and `Date`.

choices.text: The 415 for a `text/plain` body
choices.why: Right: `Accept: application/json, application/*+json` lists the media types `/books` can read.

choices.text: The 409 for a duplicate ISBN
choices.why: A conflict is described in the body, and no header lists an alternative: the fix is a different ISBN.

prompt: A client posts a book and gets a 400 whose `detail` is "Failed to read request", with no `type` and no `errors` member. What went wrong?
hint: Validation needs an object to validate.

choices.text: A field broke a constraint, and the bookshop hid which one
choices.why: A broken constraint goes through `handleMethodArgumentNotValid`, whose answer has the `invalid-request` type and an `errors` map naming the field.

choices.text: The path variable was not a number
choices.why: There is no path variable on `POST /books`, and that failure reads "Failed to convert 'id' with value...".

choices.text: The body never became a `BookRequest`, so nothing was validated
choices.why: Right. A body that is not JSON, or a value of the wrong type such as `"cheap"` for `priceCents`, fails while Jackson reads it, before `@Valid` has anything to look at.

choices.text: The ISBN is already in the catalogue
choices.why: A duplicate is found by the service, after reading and validation have both succeeded, and it answers 409.

prompt: Why does `ApiErrorHandler` override `handleMethodArgumentNotValid` instead of declaring `@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)`?
hint: The detour in the section tried the second way.

choices.text: Two handlers for one exception stop the start
choices.why: Right. Spring found two handlers for one exception in one class and failed with "Ambiguous @ExceptionHandler method mapped". Overriding changes the inherited handler's answer instead.

choices.text: An `@ExceptionHandler` method cannot return a `ProblemDetail`
choices.why: `notFound` and `duplicate` are `@ExceptionHandler` methods and return exactly that.

choices.text: The override runs before validation, so it can repair the fields
choices.why: It runs after validation has failed, with the failures in hand. Nothing here repairs a request.

choices.text: An override is cheaper than a handler lookup on every request
choices.why: Both are found once, at startup. The reason is the ambiguity, not speed.

prompt: The bookshop is sent `{"isbn": "9786500000016", "title": "Emma", "priceCents": -5}`. How many entries does the `errors` map of its 400 hold?
hint: Check each field of `BookRequest` against its constraints. The ISBN's check digit is valid, and validation runs before the service looks at the catalogue.

prompt: Why is the errors map a `TreeMap`?
hint: What did the lesson say about the order Bean Validation reports in?

choices.text: Jackson cannot write a `HashMap` as JSON
choices.why: Jackson writes any `Map`. The choice is about order, not about whether it can be written.

choices.text: So that one field can hold two messages
choices.why: A `TreeMap` holds one value per key like any other map. A field that breaks two constraints still shows one message.

choices.text: So the order is the same every time
choices.why: Right. Bean Validation reports violations in no particular order; a sorted map makes two identical requests give two identical bodies.

choices.text: Bean Validation returns the violations already sorted
choices.why: It returns them in no particular order, which is the reason for sorting them here.

prompt: Lesson 6's bad book is sent again with `Accept-Language: pt-BR`. Which message in `errors` stays in English?
hint: Which constraint declares its message as a plain sentence rather than a key?

choices.text: `must not be blank`, for the title
choices.why: `@NotBlank` is a standard constraint whose message is a key, so Hibernate Validator looked it up for Portuguese.

choices.text: `must be a valid ISBN-13`, for the ISBN
choices.why: Right. `@ValidIsbn` declares `message() default "must be a valid ISBN-13"`, a literal sentence, so there is nothing to look up in another language.

choices.text: `must be greater than or equal to 0`, for the price
choices.why: `@PositiveOrZero` is a standard constraint too, and its message came back in Portuguese.

choices.text: All of them: Bean Validation answers in English everywhere
choices.why: Spring hands Hibernate Validator the request's language, and three of the four messages came back in Portuguese.

prompt: A title of 201 spaces breaks `@NotBlank` and `@Size(max = 200)` at once. What does `errors.title` hold?
hint: The map is `Map<String, String>`, and `put` replaces.

choices.text: The `@NotBlank` message, because it is written first in `BookRequest`
choices.why: The order of annotations in the source decides nothing here; violations arrive in no particular order.

choices.text: Both messages, in a list
choices.why: That needs `Map<String, List<String>>`. With one `String` per key, the second `put` replaces the first.

choices.text: Both messages joined into one string
choices.why: Nothing joins them. `errors.put` replaces whatever the field already had.

choices.text: One of the two, and which one is not defined
choices.why: Right. Both violations are reported, the map keeps the last one `put`, and the order they arrive in is not defined.

prompt: With no handler for it, the stand-in database failure reached Spring Boot's error page. What did the client's body contain?
hint: Spring Boot's defaults decide, and the bookshop leaves them alone.

choices.text: The exception's message, with the host and the database user
choices.why: Only with `spring.web.error.include-message=always`, which the lesson turned on to show what the default keeps out.

choices.text: The stack trace
choices.why: Only with `spring.web.error.include-stacktrace=always`. By default the trace goes to the log and nowhere else.

choices.text: A timestamp, the status, its phrase and the path
choices.why: Right: `timestamp`, `status`, `error` and `path`. The message and the trace went to the second terminal.

choices.text: Nothing: a 500 is sent with an empty body
choices.why: Boot's error page writes a small JSON body, the same shape lesson 6's errors had.

prompt: The hurried catch-all answered every `Exception` with `e.getMessage()` as its detail. What went wrong? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at the response, and then at the second terminal.

choices.text: The host, the port and the database user reached the client
choices.why: Right. The exception's message was written for whoever reads the log, and the handler sent it to a stranger.

choices.text: `GET /nope` started answering 500
choices.why: It still answered 404. Spring picks the handler whose exception type is closest to the one thrown, and `NoResourceFoundException` has its own.

choices.text: Nothing was logged, so nobody running the server learnt of the failure
choices.why: Right. The exception counted as handled, so nothing reached the log, and the one person who could fix the database was the one person not told.

choices.text: The status became 200, because the exception was handled
choices.why: The handler built the problem with `HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR`, and that status is what the response carried.

prompt: Why does the bookshop keep no handler for `Exception` at all, not even one that logs and names nothing?
hint: Think about exceptions the bookshop did not write, thrown by parts of Spring that arrive in later lessons.

choices.text: Spring refuses to start with a handler for `Exception`
choices.why: It started without complaint in the detour. Only two handlers for the same type are refused.

choices.text: A handler for `Exception` would turn every 404 for a missing book into a 500
choices.why: The handler naming the closest type wins, so `BookNotFoundException` still reaches `notFound`.

choices.text: The RFC does not allow a problem document with status 500
choices.why: A problem document may carry any status. The objection is about what a catch-all catches, not about the shape.

choices.text: It would catch exceptions Spring Security expects to handle, and answer 500
choices.why: Right. Spring Security turns its refusals into 401 or 403 further out, after the controller; a catch-all in the advice gets there first. Boot's error page already logs everything and says nothing.

prompt: Put the steps of `GET /books/99` on the finished bookshop in order.
hint: The exception goes in one direction, and the answer comes back the other way.
items: The `DispatcherServlet` finds the `@ExceptionHandler` that names it
trap: The controller does not catch anything: the exception goes through it on its way to the DispatcherServlet.

prompt: A new rule: a book may not leave the catalogue while an order for it is still open. Following this lesson's design, how is the refusal built?
hint: Where does a rule live, and where does HTTP live?

choices.text: A new exception thrown by the service, mapped to 409 in `ApiErrorHandler`
choices.why: Right. The rule is the shop's, so the service states it, and one handler gives it a status and a `type` a client can compare.

choices.text: The controller looks for open orders and returns `ResponseEntity.status(409)`
choices.why: That puts the rule in the web layer, where an import job or a test calling the service would never meet it.

choices.text: The service throws an `IllegalStateException`, and Boot's error page answers it
choices.why: That would be a 500 that says nothing, for a refusal that was planned. A client could not tell it from a crash.

choices.text: The service returns a `ProblemDetail`, and the controller passes it on
choices.why: Then the service speaks HTTP, which is the coupling the lesson's first section removed.

prompt: A teammate adds `@ExceptionHandler(RuntimeException.class)` to `ApiErrorHandler`, answering a fixed 500 problem. What does `GET /books/99` answer now?
hint: `BookNotFoundException` is a `RuntimeException`, and it also has a handler of its own.

choices.text: 500, because the broader handler catches everything beneath it
choices.why: Spring does not pick the broadest handler. It picks the one whose type is closest to the exception thrown.

choices.text: The application fails to start, as with two handlers for one exception
choices.why: Only two handlers for the same type are ambiguous. `RuntimeException` and `BookNotFoundException` are different types.

choices.text: 404 from Spring Boot's error page
choices.why: Boot's error page only answers what no handler claimed, and two handlers claim this one.

choices.text: 404 from `notFound`: the closest type wins
choices.why: Right, just as `/nope` kept its 404 under the catch-all for `Exception`. The new handler only gets what nothing more specific claims.
